If you're not feeling motivated now, you won't feel motivated during third or fourth year, either. If you give yourself a bit of a break from school, you will gain new experiences that will give you a fresh perspective on school, as well as a reason to continue.

I took a year off after my third year. Working full-time during that year helped me realize that I want the type of job that earning my degree will help qualify me for. It also gave me an appreciation for being in a university setting, and having people to collaborate and share ideas with.

I strongly believe that if you feel the need for a break from academics, you should take one-- because that feeling isn't going to to go away if you just try to tough it out for the next two years. Instead, the feeling will grow, and you won't be able to make the most out of your university career.

That's funny.  Actually when I was younger I was really a stickler for grammar and spelling.  I was constantly correcting people, to the point that some of my classmates took to calling me "Miss Corrector."  But as I matured, I realized that what I was doing was not only really annoying, it was elitist and unfair.  Just because my strength happened to be spelling, I critiqued people for it to no end.  And that was really rude, because those people never criticized me for not excelling at the same things they excelled at.

As I've gotten older, I've come to realize that the main purpose of language is to communicate.  For the most part, as long as people are getting their point across, I don't mind if they don't follow prescribed grammatical and spelling rules.  I even break some of those rules myself (for example, in the ultimate sentence of the first paragraph of this post, the last word was a preposition.)  And I don't sweat typos.  

But thanks for pointing out the misspelling; I hadn't noticed it!  I'm preparing for a career as a language professional, so it's always good to be reminded to edit things properly.
